To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector $\mathbf p$ and a vector $\mathbf n$ that is perpendicular to the osculating plane. 

The position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}(0) = \cos{0}\,\mathbf i+\cos{0}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{2}\sin{0}\, \mathbf k = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle.
$$

To compute the perpendicular vector, we first need to compute the unit tangent $\mathbf T(0)$ and the principal normal $\mathbf N(0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,k)=k \\ N(0) & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0k)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =k\times (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }] \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{n} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 2}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(\mathbf i-\mathbf j\right) =\mathbf i-\mathbf j
$$

Finally, let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ denote the position vector of a general point in the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $\mathbf{p},$ its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ & =⟨1,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+0\cdot z & =0 \\ x-y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/ad/ad22c676123844c2428febb34e0218cfcb05917154e8cff994f35fa4fbf68944.png)

**Note:** Because our curve is a plane curve, it has the same osculating plane at each point. As shown above, the osculating plane coincides with the plane of the curve. 

This result holds in general: any plane curve has the same osculating plane at each of its points (wherever the osculating plane is defined).

The point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a critical point of the function $f: \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R$ if $\mathbf{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}^T.$ In such cases, we can classify $\mathbf a$ as follows:

- if $\mathbf{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, then $\mathbf a$ is a local minimum

- if $\mathbf{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, then $\mathbf a$ is a local maximum

- if $\mathbf{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A = \mathbf{f}''(\mathbf{a}).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let $\Delta_i$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if $\Delta_i > 0$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we have $\Delta_i < 0$ when $i$ is odd, and $\Delta_i > 0$ when $i$ is even.

$$

$$

The standard inner product of $\Bbb R^n,$ i.e. the dot product, does not meet the criteria of an inner product on $\Bbb C^n.$

For example, if $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is a valid inner product on $\Bbb C^n,$ then for any vector $\mathbf a \in \Bbb C^n,$ we must have

$$
\langle\mathbf a, \, \mathbf a\rangle \ge 0.
$$

But for many vectors in $\Bbb C^n,$ such as $\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ in $\Bbb C^2,$ the dot product fails to satisfy this criterion:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & ={\text{i}}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =-1 \\  & <0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Thankfully, there is an elegant way to generalize the dot product to satisfy the desired criterion on $\Bbb C^n.$ We can just take the complex conjugate of each element in the right vector before carrying out the dot product.

More formally, for two vectors $\mathbf x, \mathbf y\in \mathbb C^n$ given by

$$
\mathbf{x} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ \vdots  \\ {x}_{n}\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{y} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} \\ \vdots  \\ {y}_{n}\end{array} \right]},
$$

we define the **standard Hermitian inner product** as

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & ={x}_{1}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{2}}+⋯+{x}_{n}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{n}} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{i}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\overline{y_i}$ is the complex conjugate of $y_i.$

Using the standard Hermitian inner product instead of the dot product, our desired criterion is satisfied:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}⟩ & =\text{i}\cdot \overset{―}{\,\text{i}\,}+0\cdot \overset{―}{\,0\,} \\  & =\text{i}\cdot (-\text{i})+0\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0 \\  & =1 \\  & \ge 0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

It can be verified that the Hermitian inner product satisfies *all* the criteria of an inner product on $\Bbb C^n.$

Furthermore, since the complex conjugate leaves real numbers unchanged, the Hermitian inner product simplifies to the dot product on $\Bbb R^n.$ In other words, the dot product is just a special case of the Hermitian inner product!

We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
$$
\mathbf{a}_1={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}, \:
	\mathbf{a}_2={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}, 
	\qquad
	\mathbf{x}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}
$$
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}( \mathbf{x} - {k}_{1} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} - {k}_{2} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} ) \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} = 0 \\ ( \mathbf{x} - {k}_{1} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} - {k}_{2} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} ) \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} = 0\end{array} \right. }
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{k}_{1} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} )} + {k}_{2} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} )} = {\color{red}( \mathbf{x} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{1} )} \\ {k}_{1} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} )} + {k}_{2} {\color{blue}( {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} )} = {\color{red}( \mathbf{x} \cdot  {\mathbf{a}}_{2} )} .\end{array} \right. }
$$

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
$$
{\color{blue}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} - \\ - \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} -\end{array} \right]}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}
}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{k}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}\end{array} \right]}
	=
{\color{red}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{1} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} - \\ - \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \hspace{0.222em} \hspace{0.222em} -\end{array} \right]}
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}| \\ \mathbf{x} \\ |\end{array} \right]}
}
$$

If we denote 
$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{2} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}
$$
and $\mathbf{k}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}{k}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}\end{array} \right]},$ then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!

We’ve seen how both Euclidean and Manhattan distances can be written in terms of vector norms. These are actually special cases of a more general formula known as the **Minkowski distance**.

Given a fixed value $p \ge 1$, the Minkowski distance between two points $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in $N$-dimensional space is defined as

$$
d_p(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N |a_i - b_i|^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
$$

The corresponding **Minkowski norm** is given by

$$
\| \mathbf{v} \|_p = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N |v_i|^p \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
$$

The parameter $p$ determines how differences in individual coordinates contribute to the total distance:

- **$p=1$** (Manhattan): All differences are summed equally.

- **$p=2$** (Euclidean): Larger differences have more weight due to squaring.

- **$p \to \infty$**: The distance is determined entirely by the single largest coordinate difference.

Let’s compute an example to see how this works in practice.

Suppose $\mathbf{a} = [1,\ 2,\ 3]^T$ and $\mathbf{b} = [4,\ 0,\ 6]^T$. Let's compute their Minkowski distance using $p = 5$.

Using the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{d}_{5}(a,b) & =‖a-b{‖}_{5} \\  & ={‖\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}‖}_{5} \\  & ={(|1-4{|}^{5}+|2-0{|}^{5}+|3-6{|}^{5})}^{1/5} \\  & ={(|-3{|}^{5}+{2}^{5}+|-3{|}^{5})}^{1/5} \\  & ={(243+32+243)}^{1/5} \\  & ={518}^{1/5} \\  & ≈3.490.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's try a few examples to build intuition.

The table below describes the number of classes taken per semester and the average final grade in a sample of four college students.
Number of Courses $4$ $3$ $5$ $4$
Average Grade $80$ $85$ $75$ $72$
We can collect this data in a matrix so that each column reports the number of courses and the average grade of a single student: $$ X= {\left[ \begin{array}{cccc}4 & 3 & 5 & 4 \\ 80 & 85 & 75 & 72\end{array} \right]} $$ The matrix $X$ is called the **observation matrix.** Suppose we want to determine the mean number of courses and the mean average grade of this sample. The **sample mean vector,** denoted $\mathbf m,$ is a vector containing these values. The sample mean vector is given by $$ \mathbf{m} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{x}_i, $$ where $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n$ are the individual observations (columns of $X$). From our matrix above, we have that $$ \mathbf{x}_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}4 \\ 80\end{array} \right]}, \quad \mathbf{x}_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 \\ 85\end{array} \right]}, \quad \mathbf{x}_3 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}5 \\ 75\end{array} \right]}, \quad \mathbf{x}_4 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}4 \\ 72\end{array} \right]}. $$ Therefore, the sample mean vector is $$ \begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{4}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}) \\ & =\frac{1}{4}(\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 80\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 85\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 75\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 72\end{bmatrix}) \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 312\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 78\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ So, the average number of courses is $4,$ and the average final grade is $78.$

Recall that if the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$ 

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Therefore, the error vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A).$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

A similar property holds for weighted least-squares solutions:

*If the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf x=W\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then
$A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i,
$$

 
where the $w_i$'s are the weights from the main diagonal of the weight matrix $W.$* 

We previously considered the weighted least-squares problem $W\!Ax=W\mathbf{b},$ where

$$
A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & - 1\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
\mathbf{b} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{array} \right]}, \qquad
W = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

It's easy to show (using the usual techniques) that the unique weighted least-squares solution is given by 

$$
{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}4 \\ - 6\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Computing our error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ε & =A\hat{x}-b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ 
$$
A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}| & | \\ {\mathbf{a}}_{1} & {\mathbf{a}}_{\mathbf{2}} \\ | & |\end{array} \right]}, \qquad  \mathbf a_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{array} \right]}, \quad  \mathbf a_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 0 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]}
$$

Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3,
\quad
$$

 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as

$$
A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A).
$$

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection with respect to $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W$ of the vector $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ 

Furthermore, the weighted least-squares problem with weight matrix $W$ is equivalent to finding a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_W
$$

is as small as possible.

The **leading principal minors** of an $n\times n$ matrix are the $n$ determinants formed by the first $r$ rows and first $r$ columns of $A$ for $r = 1,2,3,\ldots, n.$ The leading principal minors of $A$ are denoted $\Delta_i.$

Note that:

- the first leading principal minors $\Delta_1$ equals $a_{11},$ and

- the $n$th leading principal minors $\Delta_n$ equals $\det(A).$

For example, consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=
	{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & - 4 \\ 6 & 9 & 8\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Since $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix, it has $3$ leading principal minors. Let's compute them:

- The first leading principal minors is the determinant formed by the first row and first column of $A:$ 
$$
{\mathrm{\Delta }}_{1} = \left| \begin{array}{c}{a}_{11}\end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{c}1\end{array} \right| = 1
$$

- The second leading principal minors is the determinant formed by the first $2$ rows and first $2$ columns of $A:$ 
$$
{\mathrm{\Delta }}_{2} = ∣ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3\end{array} ∣ = 3
$$

- The third leading principal minors is the determinant formed by the first $3$ rows and first $3$ columns of $A:$

$$
{\mathrm{\Delta }}_{3} = ∣ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & - 4 \\ 6 & 9 & 8\end{array} ∣ = 60

$$

$$

- The first leading principal minors is the determinant formed by the first row and first column of $A:$ 
$$

$$

$$
{\mathrm{\Delta }}_{3} = \left| \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & - 4 \\ 6 & 9 & 8\end{array} \right| = 60

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u+v, \: u-v, \: v\right\rangle.

$$

$$

$$

$$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then

$$

![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)

$$

$$

It's possible to derive Taylor polynomials for functions of more than two variables. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overbrace{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} \\  & \,\,+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{x}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]}$ and $\mathbf{a}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}a \\ b\end{array} \right]},$ then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

$$
𝒇'(\mathbf a) = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{f}_{x} ( a , b ) & {f}_{y} ( a , b )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x-a \\ y-b\end{bmatrix} \\  & =f(a)+\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

$$
𝒇''(\mathbf a) =
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{f}_{x x} ( \mathbf{a} ) & {f}_{x y} ( \mathbf{a} ) \\ {f}_{y x} ( \mathbf{a} ) & {f}_{y y} ( \mathbf{a} )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}x-a & y-b\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x-a \\ y-b\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\begin{bmatrix}x & y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}a & b\end{bmatrix})\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{bmatrix}\cdot (\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overbrace{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overbrace{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} \\  & \,\,+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{x}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]}$ and $\mathbf{a}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}a \\ b\end{array} \right]},$ then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

$$
𝒇'(\mathbf a) = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{f}_{x} ( a , b ) & {f}_{y} ( a , b )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x-a \\ y-b\end{bmatrix} \\  & =f(a)+\begin{bmatrix}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \left(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

$$
𝒇''(\mathbf a) =
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{f}_{x x} ( \mathbf{a} ) & {f}_{x y} ( \mathbf{a} ) \\ {f}_{y x} ( \mathbf{a} ) & {f}_{y y} ( \mathbf{a} )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}x-a & y-b\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x-a \\ y-b\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{bmatrix}x & y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}a & b\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{bmatrix}\cdot \left(\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overbrace{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$

In machine learning and linear algebra, it’s often convenient to express the Hadamard product of two vectors using matrix multiplication. If $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, then

$$
\mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{u} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{v}) \mathbf{u} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{u}) \mathbf{v}
$$

For example, given the matrix product

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]}
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]},
$$

we notice that the left matrix is diagonal. So, we can write it as a Hadamard product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} &= diag(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⊙\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now let's see a concrete example of expressing a Hadamard product as a matrix product in the next slide.

Suppose we have a system of ODEs such as

$$
\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{f}(x(t),y(t))
$$

with a nonzero equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ satisfying
$\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast) = \mathbf{0}.$

Instead of analyzing the system near a *nonzero* equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast,$ we can introduce *shifted coordinates* so that the equilibrium becomes the origin.
We define the **deviation vector**

$$
\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\ast,
$$

so that

$$
\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^\ast.
$$

This transformed system has several advantages: shifting the equilibrium to the origin makes the system easier to analyze without altering its behavior.

To illustrate, let's consider the following system of ODEs:

$$
\mathbf{x}' = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}3 & 2 \\ - 5 & 1\end{array} \right]} \mathbf{x}
+
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 6\end{array} \right]}
$$

The equilibrium point of the system is $[1, \, -1]^T.$ What is the system obtained by shifting the equilibrium to the origin?

To shift the system's equilibrium from $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$$
\displaystyle v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1+2 & -1 \\ 1 & -3+2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}-{w}_{2} &=1 \\ {w}_{1}-{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Note that the first equation is the same as the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}={w}_{2}+1.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=1,$ and therefore

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.

$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined.

$$

A vector $x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}$ belongs to ${H}^{⊥}$ if $x\cdot {h}_{1}=0$ and $x\cdot {h}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, we need to solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x\cdot {h}_{1} &=0 \\ x\cdot {h}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

 
In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd one), so ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the  second equation we get ${x}_{2}=0$ and then from the first equation we obtain  ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.$ So, any vector in ${H}^{⊥}$ has the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, $B=\{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\}$ is a basis of ${H}^{⊥}.$

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ contains ${2}^{2}=4$ elements, and is given by

$$
\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{8}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{8}(R))={8}^{2}=64.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

we have that $\text{nullity}(A)=1.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(1)\times N(1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨1,1,0⟩\times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-2\,k) \\  & =-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|\frac{1}{3}(i-j+3\,k)\cdot (-k)| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}|0+0-3\,| \\  & =\frac{|-3|}{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

$$

To find the eigenvectors, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
